title: Remotes, Fetch, Pull & Push Collaboration
description: Connect local repositories to remote hosts like GitHub, understand remote-tracking branches, and synchronize changes with fetch, pull, and push.

blocks.content: So far everything has been local. A **remote** is a copy of your repository stored somewhere else - usually on a server like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. Remotes are how teams share work and how you back up your code.

## Working with Remotes

See which remotes your project is connected to:
```
git remote -v
```

When you clone a repository, Git automatically creates a remote called `origin` pointing to where you cloned from.

## Fetching and Pulling

**Fetch** - download new commits from the remote but don't change your files yet:
```
git fetch origin
```

**Pull** - fetch AND immediately merge the remote changes into your current branch:
```
git pull
```

Pull is essentially `git fetch` followed by `git merge`. Use fetch when you want to look at what changed before merging it in.

## Pushing

Send your local commits to the remote:
```
git push origin main
```

If the remote has new commits you don't have yet, Git will refuse the push. You need to pull first, resolve any conflicts, then push.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Local Repository"] -- "git push" --> B["Remote (origin)"]
    B -- "git fetch / git pull" --> A
```

blocks.question: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
options: Fetch is faster, pull is more accurate
Fetch downloads remote changes but doesn't change your files; pull downloads and merges them
Fetch works without a network; pull requires one
They are the same command with different names
blocks.explanation: `git fetch` downloads the latest commits from the remote into your local copy but doesn't touch your working files. `git pull` does the same download and then immediately merges those commits into your current branch. Fetch is safer when you want to inspect changes before integrating them.
